Let $p \in R := K \sqbrk {x_1, \dotsc, x_n}$ be a [[Definition:Symmetric Polynomial|symmetric polynomial]].
Let $\sigma_1, \dotsc, \sigma_n$ denote the $n$ [[Definition:Elementary Symmetric Polynomial|elementary symmetric polynomials]].
Let $<$ be the [[Definition:Degree Reverse Lexicographic Monomial Order|degree reverse lexicographic monomial order]].
Let us denote by $\map {LM} f$ the [[Definition:Leading Monomial|leading monomial]] of any $f \in R$, that is to say the unique $<$-largest [[Definition:Monomial|monomial]] appearing in $f$.
Then it is straightforward to verify that $\map {LM} {\sigma_k} = x_1 \cdots x_k$ for $1 \le k \le n$:
For $k < n$, any other [[Definition:Monomial|monomial]] appearing in $\sigma_k$ must contain a factor $x_j^{\alpha_1}$ with $j > k$ and $\alpha_1 > 0$.
This makes it smaller than $x_1 \cdots x_k$ with respect to $<$.
The case $k = n$ is trivial because $\sigma_n$ consists of only one [[Definition:Monomial|monomial]].
It follows the proof that $p$ may be written as a [[Definition:Polynomial|polynomial]] in $\sigma_1, \dotsc, \sigma_k$.

Iterate this method, and after [[Definition:Finite Set|finitely many]] steps one has decomposed $p$ into a [[Definition:Polynomial|polynomial]] $F \in K \sqbrk {y_1, \dotsc, y_n}$ with $\map F {\sigma_1, \dotsc, \sigma_n} = p$.
The termination of this algorithm follows immediately from [[Dickson's Lemma]].
